claim: YouTube states that 55% of ad and subscription revenue is paid directly to creators, artists, and media companies through the YouTube Partner Program -- the only revenue-share percentage YouTube discloses on this page, and it is not broken out by long-form video vs. Shorts.
stance_target: revenue-share percentage for long-form vs Shorts monetization
scope_conditions: blended global figure across ad and subscription revenue; not decomposed by content format (long-form vs Shorts) or by country
quoted_support: 55% of ad and subscription revenue goes directly to creators, artists, and media companies through the YouTube Partner Program.
time_period: not dated on this page; page reflects 2025 impact reporting
region: not specified (implied global or US given page context)

claim: YouTube discloses a cumulative aggregate payout of over $100 billion paid to creators, artists, and media companies globally across the four years 2022-2025, sourced to YouTube first-party data -- but with no denominator (count of paid creators) given, no per-creator average or median derivable, and no distribution.
stance_target: aggregate creator payout disclosure and its insufficiency for income-distribution questions
scope_conditions: global, 2022-2025, YouTube first-party data; aggregate total only, not a per-creator distribution
quoted_support: In the past four years alone, YouTube has paid over $100 billion to creators, artists, and media companies (2022-2025). YouTube first-party data, Global, 2022-2025

claim: YouTube's creative ecosystem is stated to have contributed over $60 billion to United States GDP in 2025, per research commissioned from Oxford Economics.
stance_target: US-only macroeconomic impact claim, explicitly flagged as not generalizable to Southeast Asia
scope_conditions: United States only, 2025, third-party commissioned research (Oxford Economics); underlying methodology not published on this page
quoted_support: YouTube's creative ecosystem contributed over $60 billion to the United States's GDP in 2025. According to research by Oxford Economics, 2025
region: United States (US-only, does not generalize to Southeast Asia)

claim: YouTube's creative ecosystem is stated to have supported more than 540,000 full-time-equivalent (FTE) jobs in the United States in 2025, per Oxford Economics research commissioned by YouTube.
stance_target: US-only employment impact claim, explicitly flagged as not generalizable to Southeast Asia
scope_conditions: United States only, 2025, third-party commissioned research; FTE jobs supported across the ecosystem (not necessarily individual creators earning a living wage)
quoted_support: YouTube's creative ecosystem supported more than 540,000 full time equivalent (FTE) jobs in the United States in 2025. According to research by Oxford Economics, 2025
region: United States (US-only, does not generalize to Southeast Asia)

claim: All 50 U.S. states have at least 10 channels with over 1 million monthly views, per YouTube first-party data as of June 2025 -- a channel-count/reach claim, not an earnings or income-distribution claim.
stance_target: channel distribution breadth, not income distribution
scope_conditions: United States only, June 2025, YouTube first-party data
quoted_support: All 50 states in the U.S. have at least 10 channels with over 1 million monthly views. YouTube first-party data, US, June 2025

claim: YouTube's own promotional impact-report pages disclose no distribution of individual creator earnings, no median or mean per-creator payout, and no count of monetized (YPP) channels -- only aggregate macro totals (GDP contribution, FTE jobs, cumulative dollars paid) are published, leaving the actual income distribution across creators undisclosed by the platform.
stance_target: absence of platform-disclosed creator income distribution data -- directly relevant to the research query's core ask about median vs mean income and share earning a living wage
scope_conditions: scope limited to this specific YouTube 'How YouTube Works' impact page and its immediate methodology/report links, checked directly during fetch
quoted_support: N/A -- absence noted by the fetcher: the page provides aggregate totals ($60B GDP, 540K jobs, $100B paid, 55% revenue share) but no per-creator figures, no median/mean earnings, no monetized-channel count, and no earnings distribution anywhere on the page or its linked Impact Report entry point.
region: United States (page scope); global for the $100B figure

claim: The page's audience-facing statistics (87% of viewers watched music content, 73% say YouTube aids discovery of local history/culture, 78% of parents rate content quality positively, 94% of teachers report using YouTube content in lessons) are viewer/consumption survey findings attributed to Oxford Economics 2025, and are not creator-economics figures relevant to attrition, income, or survival questions.
stance_target: these figures should not be mistaken for creator-side economic data despite appearing on a page titled 'YouTube's Impact on the Creator Economy'
quoted_support: 87% of viewers report watching music videos, music festivals, or awards ceremonies on YouTube in the last year. According to research by Oxford Economics, 2025
